title: Candakumara's patience
hookLine: a fair prince, a grudge, and a father who believes the wrong man
tomorrow: why would a monk call the people who insult him good?

cards: Few things sting like being punished for doing the right thing. In the Jataka, Prince Canda is a fair judge. When the royal priest takes a bribe and hands down a crooked ruling, Canda sets it right in front of everyone.

The priest never forgives him. He goes to the king, Canda's own father, with a terrible plan dressed up as religion: sacrifice your sons and much of your household, and you will reach heaven. And the king believes him.
This one stays gentle: the sacrifice never happens.

teach.b: Here is where the story spends its time. Canda doesn't raise an army. He doesn't curse his father.
Led out bound, he pleads, again and again, gently.
Don't do this, father. Make us your servants. Send us away, and we'll go.

Spare the others. He never stops treating the king as his father, even when the king has stopped acting like one. That's patience under wrong, and it's harder than patience in a slow line at the store.
It isn't agreeing that the wrong is right. Canda says plainly that the plan is crooked. He just refuses to let the injustice turn him into someone else.
The tale doesn't make patience magic. The king wavers, then hardens again.

teach.h: HELP ARRIVES AT THE LAST MOMENT.
teach.b: At the last moment, the story says, Canda's wife makes a solemn act of truth, and Sakka, king of the gods, appears and stops it.
Some readers see the point there: patience held the door open long enough for help to arrive. The Dhammapada has a line for people like Canda.
In Max Müller's words: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins."

how: The Candakumara (Khandahala) Jataka is one of the last ten Jataka tales, tied by tradition to the perfection of patience, and is retold in Theravada sermons and temple art.

o: waiting your turn in a long, slow line
bearing a real injustice without turning cruel
forgiving someone because they said sorry

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: took a bribe and held a grudge
king of the gods, who stops it

s: patience under wrong means agreeing with the wrong
Canda calls the plan crooked, and stays gentle.
in the story, Canda pleads with his father again and again
he offers to be a servant, or to be sent away, to spare the others.
Canda raises an army against the king
he never stops treating the king as his father.

games.q: a teammate tells the coach you skipped practice. you didn't; you were at the dentist. the coach benches you. what's Canda's way?
o: calmly show the appointment, and keep treating the coach with respect.
say nothing at all; patience means accepting whatever happens.
skip the next practice for real, to show how unfair it was.
games.why: Canda says plainly that the plan is crooked, and keeps pleading gently. patience under wrong isn't silence, and it isn't revenge.

practice: Bring to mind one small unfairness you're carrying. Say out loud, quietly, exactly what happened, in plain words, with nothing added about the person. Then rest your hands open on your knees for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Candakumara's patience: a prince who bears a deep wrong without giving up the truth or his gentleness.

orig.note: Pali: Prince Canda, hero of Jataka 542; canda means moon, kumara a prince.

carryVoice: Keep this one: patient under wrong, which means not agreeing with it, and not becoming it either. Rest well.

sources.ref: Jataka 542, Khandahala (Candakumara) Jataka (the corrupt royal priest, the planned sacrifice, Canda's pleading, Canda's wife's act of truth, Sakka's intervention)
